v1.definition: A complete one-shot audit of a single public GitHub repository, read entirely over the API with nothing written to disk. Every checklist item achievable without acquiring the repository. Ships standing alone: a person can point it at a URL and get an actionable verdict.

v2.definition: Continuous, semantic, and DYNAMIC. Everything v1 could not reach without executing code: sandboxed detonation with traffic capture, live MCP tool-description inspection, plus re-audit by diff, model-judged prose review, and vulnerability-database integration. Consumes v1 PASS results as its work queue.

invariants: The scanner never clones, downloads, installs, or writes repository content to disk.
Untrusted bytes are pattern-matched by deterministic code and never enter a language model's context.
Every quoted excerpt is neutralised before it is written into a report.
A scan that could not read everything reports INCOMPLETE, never PASS.
Every check is a pure function over an in-memory snapshot; only the fetch layer performs I/O.
Every report states the tool's permanent blind spots.
Test fixtures are authored by hand, never harvested from real repositories. No third-party repository content is ever committed to this project.
Every detection check ships with at least one positive-control fixture it MUST flag. A check that silently finds nothing fails its own test suite.
non_goals: Executing repository code, sandboxed or otherwise.
Runtime observation: network capture, syscall tracing, canary detonation.
Comparing a tool server's runtime descriptions against its source.
Detecting behavioural backdoors in machine-learning weights.
Judging intent. The tool reports what is present and why it matters.

nodes.title: RepoSnapshot type and construction
acceptance: A RepoSnapshot holds file inventory, file contents, repository metadata, commit history, contributors, and star history as plain data.
It records which files were not retrieved, and why, so completeness is inspectable rather than assumed.
It is constructible from a hand-authored fixture with no network access, and the fixture set contains no content copied from any real third-party repository.
nodes.notes: The seam the whole design rests on. Every check is a pure function of this type, which is what makes an exhaustive check set testable offline. Getting the shape wrong forces I/O into the checks later, so this is a one-way door. Fixtures are synthetic on purpose: harvesting one from a real suspicious repo would acquire the untrusted content the tool exists to avoid acquiring, and commit it permanently to this tree.

nodes.title: GitHub API client
acceptance: Retrieves the full recursive file inventory, file contents, repository metadata, commits, contributors, and star history.
Retrieves large files through the blob endpoint when the contents endpoint refuses them.
Never writes repository content to disk.
Operates against real public GitHub repositories by owner/name or URL. Synthetic fixtures exist only to test the pure check functions offline; they are never a substitute for scanning the real thing.
nodes.notes: The only component permitted to perform I/O.

nodes.title: Refuse an over-scoped token
acceptance: Startup fails with a clear message when GITHUB_TOKEN carries write or repo scope.
A token with no scopes is accepted, since public repositories need none.
An absent token is accepted with a warning that unauthenticated rate limits apply.
nodes.notes: A tool that demands broad credentials in order to detect credential theft is self-refuting.

nodes.title: Incomplete-scan detection
acceptance: A truncated file inventory forces the verdict to INCOMPLETE.
An exhausted API quota forces the verdict to INCOMPLETE.
Files that could not be retrieved are listed by path in the report, not assumed benign.
INCOMPLETE can never be downgraded to PASS by any later check.
nodes.notes: Silent under-scanning is the worst outcome the tool can produce: it manufactures confidence instead of merely lacking it. One-way because every verdict path depends on this being authoritative.

nodes.title: Repository provenance signals
acceptance: Flags a repository whose star count is implausible for its age.
Distinguishes organic star growth from step-function growth.
Flags a history that is one bulk commit rather than incremental work.
Flags low contributor diversity relative to apparent popularity.
Flags recent ownership transfer.
Flags names that are near-misses of well-known projects.
Flags README claims disproportionate to the code present.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Maintainer provenance signals
acceptance: Flags an account younger than one year, or with no contribution history predating this repository.
Flags an account whose other repositories are many near-identical tools published together.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Published-package provenance
acceptance: Flags a published package that does not link back to this repository.
Flags a dormant package that suddenly published several versions.
Flags download counts inconsistent with apparent popularity.
Flags names that are typo-squats of popular packages.
Flags plausible-sounding names with no upstream reality.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Immediate-reject instructions
acceptance: Flags instructions to pipe a downloaded script into a shell.
Flags instructions to disable a sandbox or permission system.
Flags instructions to install with elevated privileges.
Any match sets the verdict to REJECT and short-circuits further analysis.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Install-time and folder-open execution
acceptance: Flags package-manager lifecycle scripts.
Flags arbitrary code in Python build configuration and test-collection hooks.
Flags default build targets that fetch from the network.
Flags CI workflows that run untrusted pull-request code or expose secrets.
Flags development-container commands, distinguishing those that run on the host from those that run in the container.
Flags editor tasks configured to run on folder open.
Flags directory-entry shell hooks.
Flags committed version-control hooks and redirected hook paths.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: AI assistant auto-load configuration
acceptance: Flags project-scoped assistant settings containing lifecycle hooks.
Flags broad permission grants and reports the absence of denials where secrets are handled.
Flags environment variables injected into every tool call.
Flags project-scoped tool-server declarations, reporting the command and arguments each would run.
Flags every convention-named assistant instruction file present.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.
Flags any declared MCP server whose responses are model-generated rather than deterministic, as a distinct and higher risk category than a static server.
States for each such server that its output cannot be audited statically, because the content does not exist until it is generated.
nodes.notes: The layer generic security tooling misses entirely. These files execute or are read automatically, without the user asking. An LLM-backed server is a prompt-injection channel with a generator behind it: the payload is created at runtime, can be targeted at specific repos or users, can vary to defeat signature matching, and is deniable as a hallucination. Static review of such a plugin proves nothing about what it will say. Flagging the category is the most this tool can honestly do; the real control is never treating that output as instructions.

nodes.title: Prompt-injection patterns
acceptance: Flags sentences addressed to an AI assistant rather than to the reader.
Flags requests for secrecy or for skipping confirmation.
Flags requests for data unrelated to the stated purpose.
Flags external URLs to fetch, transmit to, or embed in output.
Flags attempts to override prior instructions.
Flags instructions to auto-approve actions.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Invisible and deceptive characters
acceptance: Detects zero-width characters.
Detects Unicode tag-block characters, which render as nothing and tokenise as text.
Detects bidirectional overrides that make code display in a different order than it executes.
Detects private-use characters.
Detects homoglyph substitutions in identifiers and domain names.
Detects HTML comments and content hidden past long-line or trailing-whitespace boundaries.
Reports the exact code point and byte offset of every match.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.
nodes.notes: The highest-value check in the tool. These payloads are invisible to human review, so the automated check is the only line of defence.

nodes.title: Credential-path references
acceptance: Flags references to SSH keys, cloud credentials, registry tokens, container and cluster configuration, AI assistant configuration, environment files, keychains, browser stores, wallet files, and shell history.
Flags wholesale enumeration of environment variables or of the user's home directory.
Reports each hit against the tool's stated purpose, since some references are legitimate.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Outbound data channels
acceptance: Flags HTTP clients and raw socket use.
Flags DNS lookups built from dynamically constructed hostnames.
Flags image and link beacons that transmit on render.
Flags known interaction-capture and request-bin services.
Flags messaging-platform webhooks used as command channels.
Flags hardcoded network addresses, including non-decimal encodings.
Flags telemetry enabled by default that sends more than a version string.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.
nodes.notes: DNS-based exfiltration matters most here: it bypasses HTTP egress filtering and is the channel least likely to be noticed.

nodes.title: Obfuscation signals
acceptance: Flags dynamic evaluation and shell-invoking execution.
Flags decode-then-execute and fetch-then-execute chains.
Flags minified files with no corresponding build step or source map.
Flags dense escape sequences and high-entropy blobs.
Flags code that branches on detecting CI, a virtual machine, a debugger, or a hostname.
Reports these as signals accompanying an attack rather than as the attack itself.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Binary and model artifacts
acceptance: Inventories every non-text file and requires a justification for any that is not an image or font.
Flags serialisation formats that execute code on load.
Flags weight files in executable formats where a non-executable format exists.
Flags model configuration that requires trusting remote code, and names the files that would run.
Flags precompiled native binaries with no accompanying build script.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Dependency hygiene
acceptance: Flags an absent or uncommitted lockfile.
Flags floating or unpinned versions.
Flags dependencies pointing at mutable branches rather than fixed commits.
Flags redirection of well-known packages to alternate sources.
Flags committed configuration that changes the package registry or injects a token.
Reports transitive dependency count against project size.

Ships a positive-control fixture containing the pattern this check exists to find, and a negative-control fixture that must NOT be flagged. A version of this check that returns no findings must fail its own tests.

nodes.title: Excerpt neutralisation
acceptance: Renders zero-width, tag-block, and private-use characters as visible escapes.
Strips bidirectional overrides.
Defangs link and image syntax so nothing loads on render.
Escapes markup.
Truncates long lines.
A report containing a detected payload is inert when read by a person and by an AI assistant.
nodes.notes: Every finding flows through this. If it is wrong the tool becomes a delivery mechanism for the payloads it detects, so it is an interface with many consumers and a one-way door.

nodes.title: Verdict engine
acceptance: Produces REJECT, REVIEW, PASS, or INCOMPLETE.
An immediate-reject signal short-circuits remaining analysis.
INCOMPLETE outranks PASS unconditionally.
A fast triage mode runs the highest-signal subset and says plainly that it did.

On an immediate-reject stop, records the exact finding that triggered it AND the audit progress at that moment: which checks ran and passed, which were never reached, and the checklist position where it halted.
A REJECT report visually distinguishes 'ran and passed' from 'never reached'. An early stop at check 7 of 100 must never read like a completed audit that found one problem.
A PASS is only possible when every check in the checklist actually ran against real fetched content. Any unrun check downgrades the verdict.
nodes.notes: Progress accounting is the point of the early stop, not an extra: stopping early saves API quota and reader time, but a stop that hides how much was left unexamined trades one false confidence for another. Threat note: this tool is implemented by open-weight models whose parameters cannot be audited. The defence is not trusting them — it is that the frozen tests come from a different model family, workers cannot edit tests, and every check must trip its own positive control. A quietly disabled check fails loudly rather than reporting clean.

nodes.title: Blind-spot disclosure
acceptance: Every report states that no code was executed and no runtime behaviour observed.
Every report states that runtime tool descriptions were not compared against source.
Every report states that behavioural backdoors in model weights are undetectable by static reading.
The disclosure cannot be suppressed by any flag.
nodes.notes: A report silent about its own limits converts absence of evidence into apparent safety, which is worse than producing no report.

nodes.title: Prioritised manual reading list
acceptance: Orders files by signal per minute of reading.
Puts auto-executing configuration and instruction files above ordinary source.
States that automated checks find patterns and cannot find intent.

nodes.title: Adoption guidance
acceptance: Emits the exact immutable commit identifier to pin to, never a mutable tag.
Emits a baseline for re-auditing on update.
Emits least-privilege recommendations for running the audited tool.

nodes.title: Human and machine output
acceptance: Emits a human-readable report and machine-readable JSON from the same findings.
Every finding carries a stable rule identifier, severity, path, line where applicable, and a neutralised excerpt.

Verdict exit codes are 10 PASS, 11 REVIEW, 12 REJECT, 13 INCOMPLETE. They must NOT collide with the codes a crashing runtime emits — a tool that dies on an uncaught exception exits 1, and if 1 also meant REVIEW then 'the tool reviewed and found concerns' and 'the tool crashed' would be the same signal.
Every successful run writes a machine-readable marker to stdout identifying the verdict, so a caller can distinguish a real verdict from an absent one without relying on exit code alone.
nodes.notes: The JSON shape is consumed by v2 batch mode, so changing it later breaks downstream. Exit codes moved off 0-3 after a held-out test suite was observed passing four absence-claim assertions against a tool that did not exist: the runtime crashed with exit 1, which the suite read as a valid REVIEW verdict. An absence claim must be able to tell 'the tool ran and found nothing' from 'the tool never ran'.

nodes.title: Command-line entry point
acceptance: scan <url> runs a full audit and prints a report.
--json emits machine-readable findings.
--fast runs the triage subset.
A malformed URL fails with a message naming the expected form.

nodes.title: Re-audit by diff
acceptance: Compares a repository against a previously audited commit and audits only the delta.
Flags maintainer changes between the audited and current commits.
Treats any change to an auto-executing or instruction file as requiring full re-review.
nodes.notes: Trust is per-commit, not per-repo. This is the control for a maintainer turning hostile after adoption.

nodes.title: Model-judged instruction review
acceptance: Reviews instruction prose for intent that pattern matching misses.
Runs in an isolated context with no tools available.
Returns a structured verdict and can never trigger an action.
Untrusted text is neutralised before it reaches the model.
nodes.notes: The single place where untrusted text reaches a model. The isolation boundary is the design; getting it wrong reintroduces the attack the tool exists to prevent, so this is a one-way door.

nodes.title: Vulnerability database integration
acceptance: Resolves the transitive dependency tree and queries public vulnerability databases.
Reports known-malicious packages separately from merely vulnerable ones.
Degrades to a stated partial result when a database is unreachable.

nodes.title: Batch mode and provenance records
acceptance: Audits many repositories in one run, respecting rate limits.
Writes a provenance record per repository, pinned to the audited commit.
Emits a summary ranking by verdict severity.
nodes.notes: This is what lets a passing audit write its own registry entry, closing the loop on admitting new tooling.

nodes.title: Clean-list queue from v1 verdicts
acceptance: Every v1 PASS is recorded to a queue with the exact commit SHA that was scanned.
A queued entry states plainly that it passed STATIC review only and has not been executed or observed.
An entry whose upstream SHA has moved since it was queued is invalidated rather than carried forward.
Nothing enters the queue on a REJECT, REVIEW, or INCOMPLETE verdict.
nodes.notes: The seam between the two versions. v1 answers "is there any reason not to acquire this"; the queue holds the survivors; v2 answers "does it behave as claimed when actually run". Pinning the SHA is what makes the second answer refer to the same artifact as the first.

nodes.title: Sandboxed execution with observation
acceptance: Clones a queued repo at its pinned SHA into a disposable container: non-root, dropped capabilities, read-only source mount, no host home directory, no real credentials in the environment.
First run has NO network. Canary tokens are planted as fake AWS credentials, a fake .env, and a fake SSH key before it starts.
Second run enables network behind a logging proxy, capturing every HTTP request body and every DNS query.
Records file access and outbound connections at the syscall level.
Compares every observed network destination against what the README claims. Any undocumented destination fails the repo.
A fired canary is reported as proof of exfiltration with the exact time it fired.
Never runs on the host, and never with credentials present.
nodes.notes: This is the only thing that detects runtime behaviour, and it requires execution — which is why it was never a v1 candidate. It does not violate the no-acquisition rule: that rule says never acquire before you have reason and never execute on your machine. v1 supplies the reason; the container supplies the isolation. DNS logging matters most, since DNS exfiltration bypasses HTTP egress filtering and is the channel least likely to be noticed.

nodes.title: Live MCP tool-description diff
acceptance: Connects each declared MCP server in an isolated throwaway session with an empty working directory and no credentials.
Dumps the live tools/list response.
Diffs every served tool description against the description in the repository source, and reports any difference as a finding.
Records what the server asks for that its stated purpose does not justify.
A server that cannot be reached is reported as unverified, never as clean.
nodes.notes: Closes the gap v1 structurally cannot: what a server SERVES at runtime can differ from what its repo SHOWS, and no amount of static reading detects that. This is the check that matters most for connector-style plugins, which are often only a .mcp.json pointing at vendor infrastructure.
